etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English *dosen, from Old Norse dúsa (“to doze, rest, remain quiet”), from Proto-Germanic *dusāną (“to be dizzy”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰews- (“to fly, whirl”), from *dʰew- (“to fly, shake, reek, steam, smolder”).

Cognate with Old Frisian dusia (“to be dizzy”), German Low German dösen (“to doze”), German dösen (“to doze”), Danish døse (“to doze”), dialectal Swedish dusa (“to doze, slumber”), Icelandic dúsa (“to doze”), Old English dysiġ (“foolish, stupid”), Scots dosnit (“stunned, stupefied”), Icelandic dúra (“to nap, slumber”), also compare Dutch doezelen (“to doze”). More at dizzy.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To sleep lightly or briefly; to nap, snooze.

quote.citation: 1692, Roger L’Estrange, “ (please specify the fable number.) (please specify the name of the fable.)”, in Fables, of Æsop and Other Eminent Mythologists: […], London:  […]  R[ichard] Sare, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: If he Happen'd to Doze a little no and then in a Morning, the Jolly Cobbler Wak'd him.
I was an hour  […]  in casting up about twenty sums, being dozed with much work.

quote.citation: October 29, 1693, Robert South, a sermon preached at Christ-church in Oxford before the university
quote.text: They left for a long time (as it were) dozed and benumbed.

definitions.definition: A light, short sleep or nap.

quote.citation: 1944 September and October, A Former Pupil, “Some Memories of Crewe Works—I”, in Railway Magazine, page 285:
quote.text: Others who conscientiously attended the Technical College at night often drooped over their desks in a doze, and one does not wonder at it.
